# Summary (Clarissa)

In this project we ask whether a Chinese tea's caffeine level can be used to predict its category. 
The dataset has eight categories: green, white, yellow, oolong, black, dark, pu'er and scented tea. 
Using The [Chinese Tea Dataset](https://chinatea.house/dataset/), which describes 136 named Chinese teas, 
we train a **\[insert method here when we decided, e.g. decision tree / logistic regression\]** classifier that uses caffeine level 
(low, moderate or high) as its predictor. We compare it against a baseline that always predicts the most common category 
(oolong, 25% of teas). **\[insert final result here\]**. This matters because shops and drinkers often treat the tea types 
as a guide to caffeine levels. If category cannot be recovered from caffeine, that rule of thumb is unreliable, and people 
limiting caffeine should not rely on tea type alone.

The main limitations are the following:
1.  Caffeine is recorded as a coarse three-level label rather than a measured amount, and most teas (69%) are labelled "moderate".
2.  A model using caffeine alone can therefore identify at most three categories, which caps accuracy at about 41%.
3.  The dataset is small, two categories are rare (4 yellow and 9 dark teas), and several teas appear twice under different spellings.



# Introduction (Clarissa)
Tea is a major source of caffeine and is highly consumed in China. 
Caffeine intake of up to 400 mg per day does not raise health concerns for healthy adults ([Yong et al., 2022](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35513285/)), but people who are sensitive to caffeine, or who need to limit it, have to judge how much they are taking in. 
Tea drinkers often use a tea's category as a rough guide, assuming for example that white and green teas are low in caffeine and black teas are high. However, caffeine content varies with tea variety, geographical origin 
and season ([Zhang et al., 2022](https://www.maxapress.com/article/id/62e78ad3ce60b94f990b397f)), and a nationwide study of Chinese teas found that average caffeine content differed only modestly between categories, from about 27 mg/g for oolong to 43 mg/g for yellow tea ([Yong et al., 2022](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35513285/)).

In this project, we use a machine learning algorithm to predict a Chinese tea's category (for example green, oolong or black tea) given its caffeine level. 
Answering this question is important because it tests how reliable category is as a guide to caffeine. If caffeine level strongly predicts category, the two carry overlapping information and category is a reasonable shortcut. 
If it does not, the common rule of thumb is unreliable, and people limiting their caffeine should look for caffeine information directly rather than relying on tea type.

To answer this question, we use [The Chinese Tea Dataset](https://chinatea.house/dataset/). It contains 136 named Chinese teas, such as Xi Hu Longjing and Menghai 7542, each described by 11 columns:
an identifier, English and Chinese names, category, growing region, caffeine level, body, oxidation level, main flavour notes, a short written description and a tier. 
Caffeine level is recorded as one of three values: low, moderate or high. The target we want to predict is the tea's category, which has eight classes: green, white, yellow, oolong, black, dark, pu'er and scented tea.
